parsing_res_list.block_content: Gas Properties: We assume the gas initially traces the soliton potential in hydrostatic equilibrium.

Cooling Time and Multiphase Scaling: The cooling timescale is given by  $ t_{\text{cool}} \sim \frac{k_B T}{n \Lambda(T)} $. Given  $ n \propto M_s^4 $ and  $ T \propto M_s^2 $, the scaling depends on the cooling function  $ \Lambda(T) $:

• Atomic Cooling Threshold ( $ T < 10^4 $ K): For  $ M_s < 2.8 \times 10^7 M_\odot $,  $ \Lambda(T) $ is exponentially suppressed by the Boltzmann factor. Consequently,  $ t_{\text{cool}} $ increases sharply as  $ M_s $ decreases, exceeding the dynamical time and creating a stable regime.
- Line Cooling Regime  $ (10^4 < T < 10^7 \text{ K}) $: As implemented in our numerical model,  $ \Lambda(T) \propto T^{-0.6} $ in this interval. The scaling becomes:
This explains the shallower slope of the cooling curve in the middle section of Figure 2.

- Bremsstrahlung Regime  $ (T > 10^7 \text{ K}) $: For massive cores  $ (M_s \sim 10^9 M_\odot) $, thermal bremsstrahlung dominates, so  $ \Lambda(T) \propto T^{1/2} $. Substituting the scalings yields:
This confirms the steep slope  $ t_{\mathrm{cool}} \propto M_s^{-3} $ shown in Figure 2 for the high-mass regime.
Comparing the slopes derived above against the dynamical support:
- Radiative Cooling:  $ t_{\text{cool}} \propto M_s^{-0.8} $ (intermediate) and  $ t_{\text{cool}} \propto M_s^{-3} $ (high-mass)
The intersection  $ t_{dyn} = t_{cool} $ defines the stability limit. Numerically solving for our fiducial parameters  $ (m_{22} = 2.0) $, we find a critical mass scale:

For  $ M_s > M_{\text{crit}} $, the gas loses thermal energy faster than the potential can dynamically readjust  $ (t_{\text{cool}} < t_{\text{dyn}}) $. This leads to catastrophic collapse rather than a static hot atmosphere, confirming the “Opacity Crisis”.
